sbh2.6:1.2: Mindfulness having in-and-out-breaths as its object — this is called *ānāpānasmṛti*.
sbh2.6:2.5: The in-breath is the air that, immediately after the out-breath, moves inward as far as the navel region.
sbh2.6:2.6: The inner-in-breath is, when the in-breath has ceased and the out-breath has not yet arisen, the brief intervening air at the resting-place that arises in a similar manner.
sbh2.6:2.8: The out-breath and inner-out-breath should be understood likewise.
sbh2.6:2.10: the air moves outward from the navel region as far as the tip of the mouth or nose, and from there outside.

sbh2.6:3.3: Karmic action conditioned by the body, and the cavity of the navel region;
sbh2.6:3.4: or alternatively, the cavity of the body that arises from this.
sbh2.6:3.5: What are the two supports of in-and-out-breathing?
sbh2.6:3.9: and proceed accordingly. If they were body-supported only,
sbh2.6:3.10: they would proceed in beings attained to the unconscious attainment, the cessation attainment, and in beings born among the unconscious gods.
sbh2.6:3.12: they would proceed in beings attained to or born in the formless attainments.
sbh2.6:3.13: If they were body-and-mind-supported in the simple sense,
sbh2.6:3.14: they would proceed in beings attained to the fourth absorption and in beings in the *kalala* (zygote), *arbuda* (early embryo), and *peśī* (fleshy mass) stages of gestation.
sbh2.6:3.15: But they do not so proceed.
sbh2.6:3.16: Therefore in-and-out-breaths are body-supported and mind-supported in a specifically conditioned sense, and proceed accordingly.

sbh2.6:7.1: Five familiarities of this *ānāpānasmṛti* should be known:
sbh2.6:7.2: counting-familiarity, aggregate-entry-familiarity, dependent-origination-entry-familiarity, truth-entry-familiarity, and sixteen-aspect-familiarity.
sbh2.6:8.3: with mindfulness bound to the in-and-out-breath, he counts 'one.'
sbh2.6:8.4: When the in-breath has ceased and the out-breath arises and goes out,
sbh2.6:8.5: he counts 'two.' Thus he counts up to ten.
sbh2.6:8.6: This counting is neither too compressed nor too extended. This is called one-by-one counting.
sbh2.6:8.8: When the in-breath has entered and ceased,
sbh2.6:8.11: By this method of counting he counts up to ten.
sbh2.6:8.13: He combines in-and-out into a single unit and counts it as one — thus called two-as-one counting.
sbh2.6:8.15: By either one-by-one counting or two-as-one counting, he counts forward up to ten.
sbh2.6:8.18: Starting from ten in reverse — nine, eight, seven, six, five — down to one.
sbh2.6:8.20: When, relying on one-by-one counting or two-as-one counting, he has made familiarity with forward and reverse counting,
sbh2.6:8.21: and the mind does not become distracted in the meantime,
sbh2.6:8.23: then his subsequent superior counting is described.
sbh2.6:8.25: By either one-by-one or two-as-one counting, he makes two-as-one and counts.
sbh2.6:8.26: By two-as-one counting, four in-and-out-breaths are one unit.
sbh2.6:8.27: By one-by-one counting, an in-and-out pair is one. Thus he counts up to ten.
sbh2.6:8.28: By such progressive enlargement, he eventually makes a hundred breaths one unit and counts.
sbh2.6:8.29: Then by hundred-as-one counting in sequence he counts up to ten.
sbh2.6:8.30: When this counting-engaged practitioner makes ten-as-one and counts up to ten —
sbh2.6:8.31: as long as he fulfills the ten —
sbh2.6:8.32: by this ten-as-one counting the mind does not become distracted afterward.
sbh2.6:8.33: By this much, his counting-familiarity is accomplished.
sbh2.6:8.34: Of this counting-engaged practitioner, if the mind becomes distracted in the meantime, he turns back and starts counting again from the beginning,
sbh2.6:8.36: When his mind, by its own nature (*svarasa*), goes along the inner path of natural movement — having mounted onto the in-and-out-breath object — uninterrupted, without gap, taking the in-breath as it proceeds, taking the empty-of-out-breath state when the in-breath has ceased, taking the out-breath as it proceeds, taking the cessation when it ceases — unwavering, unmoving, without aspect of distraction, and accompanied by delight —
sbh2.6:8.37: by this much the counting-stage is transcended.
sbh2.6:8.38: Then no more counting is to be done.
sbh2.6:8.39: Mind is no longer bound to any object other than the in-and-out-breaths.
sbh2.6:8.40: The in-and-out-breaths — together with the inner pauses, and with their states of arising and ceasing — are to be followed and characterized.
sbh2.6:8.42: This counting-familiarity is prescribed for those of dull faculties.
sbh2.6:8.43: For them, [the breath alone] is a place of distraction.
sbh2.6:8.44: For mental abiding, for mental enjoyment, [counting is needed];
sbh2.6:8.45: without counting, sloth-and-torpor would overcome them, or the mind would be distracted outwardly — counting-engagement prevents this.
sbh2.6:8.46: But for those of sharp faculties, with quick understanding, the use of counting becomes too elementary.
sbh2.6:8.47: Once instructed, they penetrate the counting-engagement very quickly,
sbh2.6:8.48: and do not find delight in it.
sbh2.6:8.49: They bind mindfulness to the in-and-out-breath object, and concerning *where* it proceeds, *how far* it proceeds, *in what manner* it proceeds, and *when* it proceeds —
sbh2.6:8.50: they investigate and characterize all of it with established mindfulness.
sbh2.6:8.51: This is the form of their engagement.
sbh2.6:8.52: Through familiarization, cultivation, and frequent practice of this engagement, bodily pliancy and mental pliancy arise.
sbh2.6:8.53: He attains one-pointedness and emerges with delight in the object.
sbh2.6:9.1: He who has thus made counting-familiarity, by attending to the matter of grasper-and-grasped, enters the aggregates.
sbh2.6:9.2: The in-and-out-breaths, and that body which is their support — attending to these, he enters the form-aggregate.
sbh2.6:9.3: The experience-and-undergoing of those in-and-out-breaths, conjoined with the mindfulness that grasps them — this he enters as the feeling-aggregate.
sbh2.6:9.4: The cognizing of them — this he enters as the perception-aggregate.
sbh2.6:9.5: The mindfulness, the volition, and the discernment present here —
sbh2.6:9.6: this he enters as the formations-aggregate.
sbh2.6:9.7: The mind, mentation, consciousness — this he enters as the consciousness-aggregate.
sbh2.6:9.9: thus having entered the aggregates — this is called aggregate-entry-familiarity.
sbh2.6:10.1: When through this he has seen mere aggregate,
sbh2.6:10.2: fully understood it as mere formation, mere substance, then he enters the dependent origination of these very formations.
sbh2.6:10.4: He searches and seeks: 'These in-and-out-breaths — supported by what? Conditioned by what?'
sbh2.6:10.5: It occurs to him: 'These in-and-out-breaths are body-supported, body-conditioned; mind-supported, mind-conditioned.
sbh2.6:10.6: The body and the mind — what are they conditioned by?'
sbh2.6:10.7: He enters: 'The body and the mind are conditioned by the life-faculty.'
sbh2.6:10.9: he enters: 'The previous-formation is conditioned by ignorance.'
sbh2.6:10.10: Thus: ignorance-conditioned previous-formation; the previous-formation conditioning all formations is the life-faculty; the life-faculty-conditioned body, and consciousness; the body-and-mind-conditioned in-and-out-breaths.
sbh2.6:10.11: From the cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations.
sbh2.6:10.12: From the cessation of formations, cessation of the life-faculty.
sbh2.6:10.13: From the cessation of the life-faculty, cessation of body-and-mind.
sbh2.6:10.14: From the cessation of body-and-mind, cessation of in-and-out-breaths.
sbh2.6:10.16: Frequently abiding in this, he is said to have made familiarity in the dependent-origination aspect.
sbh2.6:11.1: Having thus made familiarity in dependent origination: 'These formations which are dependently arisen —
sbh2.6:11.3: Because of impermanence: not having been, they pass away.
sbh2.6:11.4: Again, not having been, they come to be;
sbh2.6:11.5: having come to be, they pass away.
sbh2.6:11.6: They are subject to birth, aging, illness, death.
sbh2.6:11.7: What is subject to birth, aging, illness, death — that is suffering. What is suffering — that is not-self, not autonomous, devoid of master.
sbh2.6:11.8: Thus by the aspects of impermanent, suffering, empty, and not-self, he has entered the truth of suffering.
sbh2.6:11.9: Whatever arising there is of these formations —
sbh2.6:11.10: that is suffering-become, illness-become, ulcer-become; all of it conditioned by craving.
sbh2.6:11.11: Whatever the complete abandoning of this craving that gives rise to suffering — this is peace, this is excellent, this is [the path] — knowing thus, abiding frequently thus, the complete abandoning of craving will come to be.
sbh2.6:11.12: Thus he enters the truth of arising, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
sbh2.6:11.13: Frequently abiding in this — when he comprehends the truths —
sbh2.6:12.1: For one who has thus made familiarity in the truths,
sbh2.6:12.2: with the abandoning of dharmas to be abandoned by seeing, the dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation remain.
sbh2.6:12.3: For their abandoning, he makes the sixteen-aspect-familiarity.
sbh2.6:13.2: Mindful while breathing in: he trains 'I breathe in mindful.'
sbh2.6:13.3: Mindful while breathing out: he trains 'I breathe out mindful.'
sbh2.6:13.4: Long. Short. Experiencing the whole body.

sbh2.6:13.6: Breathing out experiencing the whole body,

sbh2.6:13.10: Experiencing rapture; experiencing happiness — he trains.
sbh2.6:13.11: Experiencing the mental-formation; calming the mental-formation, breathing in: he trains 'I breathe in calming the mental-formation.'
sbh2.6:13.12: Breathing out, he trains 'I breathe out calming the mental-formation.'
sbh2.6:13.14: Gladdening the mind; concentrating the mind; liberating the mind, breathing in: he trains 'I breathe in liberating the mind.'
sbh2.6:13.15: Breathing out, he trains 'I breathe out liberating the mind.'
sbh2.6:13.16: Contemplating impermanence; contemplating abandoning; contemplating dispassion; breathing in: he trains 'I breathe in contemplating cessation.'
sbh2.6:13.17: Breathing out, he trains 'I breathe out contemplating cessation.'
sbh2.6:14.1: What is the distinction of these?
sbh2.6:14.3: the trainee, accomplished in seeing, becomes capable
sbh2.6:14.4: of attending to the four foundations of mindfulness with the in-and-out-breath as object;
sbh2.6:14.6: for the abandoning of the remaining fetters.
sbh2.6:14.8: Breathing in, he trains 'I breathe in mindful.'
sbh2.6:14.9: When he takes the in-breath or out-breath as object, he trains 'I breathe in long, I breathe out long.'
sbh2.6:14.10: When he makes the inner-in-breath or inner-out-breath the object,
sbh2.6:14.11: he trains 'I breathe in short, I breathe out short.'
sbh2.6:14.12: Thus indeed the in-and-out-breaths proceed long;
sbh2.6:14.13: the inner-in-breaths and inner-out-breaths are short, and proceed accordingly.
sbh2.6:14.16: When he resolves on the in-and-out-breaths reaching the subtle-cavity-state, penetrating into [the body's] dispersion,
sbh2.6:14.17: he makes [the whole body] the object.
sbh2.6:14.18: When the out-breath has ceased and the inner-out-breath is present,
sbh2.6:14.19: when the in-breath has not yet arisen and the inner-in-breath is present,
sbh2.6:14.20: he makes the empty-of-breath state — the state separated from breath, the state obstructed by [its absence], the white state — the object.
sbh2.6:14.21: At that time, calming the body-formation, breathing in — he trains 'I breathe in calming the body-formation.'
sbh2.6:14.22: Breathing out, he trains 'I breathe out calming the body-formation.'
sbh2.6:14.23: Through familiarization, cultivation, and frequent practice —
sbh2.6:14.24: those rough, unpleasant-to-touch in-and-out-breaths that proceeded for one previously not familiar —
sbh2.6:14.25: for the familiarized one, other breaths proceed: soft, pleasant-to-touch.
sbh2.6:14.26: Therefore he says, 'calming the body-formation, I breathe in' — he trains.

sbh2.6:15.3: If he is one who attains

sbh2.6:15.6: Beyond the third absorption, *ānāpānasmṛti* is no longer applicable.

sbh2.6:16.1: Of this practitioner — experiencing rapture, or experiencing happiness —
sbh2.6:16.2: if at some time, due to occasional loss of mindfulness, [confusion] arises:
sbh2.6:16.3: 'I am,' or 'this very I am,' 'I shall be' or 'I shall not be,' 'I shall be with form, I shall be without form,'
sbh2.6:16.5: 'I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient' — when such confusion-perception-volition-accompanied agitation, conceptual fabrication, and craving-laden formed state arises,

sbh2.6:16.11: Thus, 'experiencing the mental-formation, calming the mental-formation, breathing in, I breathe in calming the mental-formation' — he trains.
sbh2.6:17.1: If he is one who attains the basic first, second, or third absorptions, and is necessarily an attainer of the access (*anāgamya*) of the first absorption,
sbh2.6:17.2: taking that as support, he reviews his arisen mind:
sbh2.6:17.3: with passion or without passion; with hatred or without; with delusion or without; contracted, slack, exalted-or-not, calmed-or-not, concentrated-or-not, well-cultivated-or-not, liberated-or-not — thus he knows the mind as-it-actually-is.
sbh2.6:17.6: When the mind is fixed on the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor,
sbh2.6:17.7: gathering it inwardly, he displays one or another inspiring object,
sbh2.6:17.12: When he sees [the mind] checked by the hindrance of agitation, the hindrance of remorse,
sbh2.6:17.13: drawing it up, he displays one or another inspiring object, establishes it inwardly.
sbh2.6:17.16: When through familiarization, cultivation, and frequent practice that mind has become distanced from the active occurrence of hindrances,
sbh2.6:17.18: therefore 'liberating the mind, breathing in, I breathe in liberating the mind' — he trains.
sbh2.6:18.1: Of the one whose mind is liberated from the hindrances obstructive to path-cultivation, the latent tendencies remain.
sbh2.6:18.3: For their abandoning, he confronts the path — namely, he carefully, properly, and wisely examines the impermanence of formations.
sbh2.6:18.5: Supported by either the first, second, or third absorption, or by access — [previously] the *śamatha* engagement.
sbh2.6:18.6: Now, engaging directly in the contemplation of impermanence, he engages in *vipaśyanā*. Thus his mind, perfumed by *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, is liberated in the elements,
sbh2.6:18.9: The element of abandoning, the element of dispassion, and the element of cessation.
sbh2.6:18.10: The abandoning of all formations to be abandoned by seeing — that is the abandoning-element.
sbh2.6:18.11: The abandoning of all formations to be abandoned by cultivation — that is the dispassion-element.
sbh2.6:18.12: The cessation of all bases of clinging — that is the cessation-element.
sbh2.6:18.13: Thus, attending to the three elements as peace, as security, as health, he cultivates *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
sbh2.6:18.14: Through familiarization, cultivation, and frequent practice, the mind is liberated from the remaining cultivation-abandonable defilements.
sbh2.6:18.15: Therefore 'contemplating abandoning, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, breathing in, I breathe in contemplating cessation' — he trains.
sbh2.6:19.1: Thus, when the defilements abandonable by seeing and by cultivation
sbh2.6:19.2: have been abandoned, he becomes an arhat,
sbh2.6:19.3: one whose outflows are exhausted. There is nothing further to be done by him.
sbh2.6:19.4: Or there is only familiarity with what has been done.
sbh2.6:19.6: And this is the fivefold familiarity.
sbh2.6:20.1: Where a person of discursive-thought temperament is engaged, he engages with delight.
sbh2.6:20.3: with [bringing of] inwardness, near-and-near in the inmost — hereby, the agitation of discursive thought that would arise for one engaging does not arise.
sbh2.6:20.4: The mind quickly settles on the object;
sbh2.6:20.7: This is the fivefold purifying-conduct object for the discursive-temperament person.
